archetype.name: Gunslinger (reined-in backup)
archetype.definition: A big-armed, historically turnover-prone passer whose Seattle role has him working a run-first, play-action offense built around one star receiver, with the risk dialed down.

report.headline: A brilliant 48-attempt sample that his career and his shotgun splits don't support
report.take:
Drew Lock's 2026 file reads like a different quarterback from the one in his career rows. His 0.451 EPA per dropback ranks 2nd of 45 and his +6.72 CPOE ranks 5th. In five previous seasons his best EPA per play was 0.104 as a 2019 rookie, and his CPOE was negative every year, bottoming out at -6.1 with the 2024 Giants. The logged sample here is two games and 48 attempts, one of them relief work behind Sam Darnold in Week 1. That is enough to say he played well in this system. It is not enough to say he has changed.

The cause is fairly clear: Seattle made the game easy for him. The Seahawks pass well below expectation (-7, 28th) behind a defense that ranks 2nd in EPA, so Lock rarely had to carry a game. Under center, which in this offense means play-action, he went a perfect 14 for 14 with a +29.7 CPOE and 13.4 EPA. One receiver did most of the rest. Jaxon Smith-Njigba's 21 targets produced 24.7 EPA, more than Lock's entire dropback total of 24.3. Everyone else he threw to added up to roughly nothing, and Rashid Shaheed's targets were a net loss.

The split that matters most is shotgun. From the gun his completion rate drops to 61.8%, his CPOE is -2.5 and his success rate is 0.371. That is close to the career Lock: functional, streaky, and dependent on the big play. The deep numbers (9.9 EPA on 5 attempts) and the zero interceptions are the most fragile parts of the line. This is a passer whose 2020 season had 15 picks, 58th of 59, and a 22.1% bad-throw rate. His 12.5% bad-throw rate this year is a real improvement, but it rests on a small base.

His season has also turned. He is listed Out with an elbow injury, served only as the emergency third quarterback in Week 7, and sits at QB2 after Darnold reclaimed the start. Lock is now insurance. When he does play, expect something between the two versions of him: a competent game-script quarterback in a run-heavy offense, not a top-two efficiency passer.

strengths.title: Play-action under center is lethal
strengths.body: From under center he completed every attempt, with a +29.7 CPOE and more EPA than he produced from the shotgun on fewer than half the plays. That is scheme: Macdonald's run-first approach sets up clean, defined throws off play fakes. The perfect line won't hold, but the structure that creates it will, and it is the best way to use him.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba efficiently
strengths.body: Lock funneled 21 targets to Smith-Njigba at 1.178 EPA per target. That is the right decision, and a repeatable one, because the elite option is obvious. The rate will cool, but the habit of working the No. 1 read rather than forcing elsewhere is a better process than he showed in Denver.

strengths.title: Cleaner ball than his history
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate of 12.5% is below every career season on file, and he has no turnover-worthy plays. Part of that is a shorter, more defined menu (7.69 intended air yards). Part of it may be genuine growth at 30. It is worth trusting a little, not a lot.

concerns.title: Career says the efficiency regresses
concerns.body: A +6.72 CPOE from a passer who was negative in all five prior seasons, on 48 attempts, is the textbook sample-size outlier. Wins over NE and an ARI defense now ranked 27th helped too. Expect his completion percentage over expected to drift back toward zero.

concerns.title: Shotgun Lock looks like old Lock
concerns.body: When the offense can't lean on play-action, he is a sub-40% success-rate passer with a negative CPOE. In trailing scripts or obvious passing downs he loses the scheme crutch, and his red-zone accuracy (-6.3 CPOE) already shows the tighter windows biting.

concerns.title: Elbow and a lost job
concerns.body: He is listed Out with an elbow injury and sits behind Darnold at QB2. His playing time now depends on someone else's health. The line he did post also leans heavily on deep shots (5 attempts, 9.9 EPA) that are the first thing a sore throwing elbow and a small sample take away.

trend.note: The two logged games climbed from 6.4 EPA in relief in Week 1 to 16.1 in his Week 2 start at Arizona. The elbow injury then stopped the run, and Darnold has the job back.

nextGame.headline: Great matchup for a deep thrower, if he even takes a snap
nextGame.body:
On paper, Chicago is exactly the defense Lock's best throws exploit. The Bears allow the most deep EPA in the league (32nd) and the 30th-ranked explosive pass rate, while staying stingy underneath (5th in short EPA). That rewards play-action shots to Smith-Njigba over the dink-and-dunk game. The catch is their 3rd-ranked sack rate, which collides with a Seattle line that already allows the 30th-ranked hit rate.

Availability dominates. Lock carries an Out tag with an elbow injury, was only the emergency third QB in Week 7, and is QB2 behind Darnold, so he plays only in relief. Left tackle Charles Cross (98% of snaps) is doubtful with a high ankle sprain, which makes the Bears' rush more dangerous for whoever starts. On Chicago's side, LB T.J. Edwards (88% of snaps) is out, which softens the middle of the field. Corner Malik Muhammad II (75%) is questionable, which bears directly on Smith-Njigba's matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Play-action shots vs worst deep defense
keyMatchups.body: Lock's deep attempts were his biggest EPA source, and Chicago bleeds deep EPA more than any defense. If Seattle sells the run and he gets time, this is where a relief appearance could produce.

keyMatchups.title: Bears rush vs Cross-less line
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's sack rate ranks 3rd and Cross is doubtful. Seattle already gets its passer hit at one of the league's highest rates, and Lock's shotgun play is where pressure hurts him most.

keyMatchups.title: Smith-Njigba vs depleted Bears secondary
keyMatchups.body: Chicago has held WR1s only around their averages (20th), and Muhammad's toe adds doubt at corner. Anything Lock does here runs through his top target.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock is active and upgraded from Out to QB2, which tells you if the elbow is healed enough to be real insurance behind Darnold.

restOfSeason.body:
As a backup, Lock's rest of season is a contingency. If he starts again, the run-first structure, the elite defense and Smith-Njigba will keep him useful. The 0.451 EPA per dropback, the perfect interception line and the deep-ball efficiency will not survive more volume, given five seasons of negative CPOE and a shotgun profile that already looks like his old self. A fair expectation in a start is about 185-235 passing yards and one or two touchdowns, with efficiency just above average rather than near the top.

The parts that should last are the play-action effectiveness and the tighter decision-making with one dominant target. The parts that should fade are the completion rate, the TD rate, and the turnover-free line. Losing Cross for any stretch raises his sack and turnover risk in whatever snaps he plays.

confidence.note: 48 attempts, an elbow injury, and a backup role behind Darnold.
